title: I Posted the Community-Theater Fly-Rail Hours After They Cut My Cue

parts.text: I stepped into rail two at 6:06 p.m. and director Leni was already using my numbered line. The board said: ONE CUE. NINETY MINUTES. LINES STAY WITH THE BOOKING. I was twenty-eight, fly captain, holding a clipboard that listed our cue. Leni shrugged. "Directors are the rail." I photographed the board, the booking, and her hand on my line. Then I asked for the rail hours. At 6:14 the stage desk pinged why Leni's hand sat on our line. I kept my voice indoor and let the timestamp talk. A paper policy is only paper until someone treats it like a clock.
parts.cliffhanger_hint: The stage desk can see Leni's hand on rail two during our cue.

social.video_title: She cut my numbered fly-rail cue — Part 1/2
social.description: Community theater, a director on my line, a ninety-minute clock she posted. I logged the hand. Would you have asked for the rail hours?

parts.text: Leni called it spike marks until the desk asked for the photo. I printed the ticket, the board, and the rail still. The line went back to my numbered pin. Leni ran a slot of their own and told the next director atmosphere was always about optics. Optics is a word people use when a booking exists. Policy now has a second line: DIRECTORS ARE NOT THE RAIL. I keep our cue on a labeled card. Leni brown-bags her hands. The rail finally looks like a booking, not a loan. The rule looks ordinary now, which is the whole point.

social.video_title: Directors are not the rail — Part 2/2
social.description: Rail hours, numbered line, and a second line on the board. Were spike marks ever our cue?
